blocks.content: ETHAN
I walked without a plan, which sounds like I'm a free spirit. I'm not. I've just learned that planning a painting is the fastest way to make a bad one.

I stopped at the alley on Clement. There's a faded mural there from some festival years ago — the color's gone thin in places but the composition is still good. Ivy splitting the wall in uneven lines. The kind of accidental geometry you can't manufacture.
I was about to set up when I heard laughter from down the street.
I knew before I looked. Which I am aware is insane. I'd heard her laugh once. Once. I had absolutely no business recognizing it.
But I did.

She was crossing toward the park with her friend, the dinosaur still tucked under one arm. She moved through the street the way some people do — like she was collecting details for later, not just passing through.
As a person who makes a living noticing things, I noticed this about her immediately and found it deeply inconvenient.
Don't stare.
I stared.
And then — because apparently the universe has a sense of timing — she turned.

Half a second of eye contact. Maybe less. She smiled — quick, bright, thrown across the street like she had extras to spare — and I looked down and pretended to search my bag for something I definitely did not need.
When I looked up she was walking away.
The smile wasn't.
CASSANDRA

The guy near the alley had the look of someone who'd been caught doing something very minor and very accidental. Bag on one shoulder, coffee in hand, going through his bag like he'd just remembered something urgent that definitely wasn't there.
I'd seen him through the café window earlier. Sketchbook guy. I'd clocked him for half a second and then made myself stop clocking him, which — fine. I am only human.
I smiled. It was automatic. I smile at people.

blocks.speaker: Lena
blocks.content: Who are you smiling at?

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: No one.

blocks.speaker: Lena
blocks.content: That was not a no-one smile.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: There are categories?

blocks.speaker: Lena
blocks.content: There are absolutely categories. That was at minimum a someone-adjacent smile.

blocks.speaker: Cassandra
blocks.content: He was just standing there.

blocks.speaker: Lena
blocks.content: Men do be standing.

I glanced back once. He was already walking the other direction, head down, shoulders tucked in slightly — the posture of someone who'd decided long ago they were taking up too much space and kept trying to correct for it.
I know that posture. Not pity — I hate pity. More like recognition. The kind where you see someone doing the thing you also do and think: oh. You too.
